title: Bismarck Edits the Ems Dispatch
text:
In July 1870 France was alarmed that a Hohenzollern prince, a relative of the Prussian king, had been offered the Spanish throne. Under French pressure the candidacy was withdrawn. But the French government wanted more, and on 13 July its ambassador, Vincent Benedetti, approached King Wilhelm I of Prussia on the promenade at the spa town of Bad Ems. He asked for a guarantee that the candidacy would never be renewed. The king politely declined and later sent word that he had nothing more to say on the subject.

A report of the encounter was telegraphed to the Prussian chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, in Berlin, with permission to publish it. Bismarck believed a war with France was coming and that it would unite the German states behind Prussia, but only if France appeared to be the aggressor. In his memoirs he describes how, at dinner with the generals Moltke and Roon, he shortened the text. Without adding anything, he cut it so that it read as if the king had abruptly dismissed the ambassador and refused to see him again.

Bismarck wrote that the edited version would have the effect of a red rag on the Gallic bull. It was released to the press and foreign governments. In Paris, public opinion was outraged at the supposed insult, and on 19 July 1870 France declared war on Prussia. The southern German states joined Prussia. Within months France was defeated, and in January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed.
lesson: Words can be shaped to provoke the reaction you want, so read official messages critically. A side that loses its temper can be maneuvered into the role of aggressor.
people: Otto von Bismarck, Wilhelm I, Vincent Benedetti, Napoleon III
source: Otto von Bismarck, Thoughts and Reminiscences (Gedanken und Erinnerungen), vol. 2
caveat: Bismarck wrote his memoirs decades later and may have dramatized his own role.
